Materiality is a decision, not a catalogue
A long list can describe the business without identifying what can materially change its outcome. The materiality 
process narrows attention to issues capable of significant effect, considering both AXISCADES’ impact on 
stakeholders and the effect of the issue on enterprise value. The result should guide ownership, risk response, 
capital, target setting and disclosure.
The eight-matter working view reflects the current strategy and operating transition. It is not permanent. A matter 
can become more or less material as the business perimeter, manufacturing footprint, regulation, technology, 
customer expectations or stakeholder consequence changes.
Assess impact and enterprise value together
Stakeholder impact considers the scale, scope, likelihood and remediability of positive or negative effects on 
people, the environment and society. Enterprise-value relevance considers the potential effect on revenue, cost, 
cash, capital, asset value, access to markets, resilience and reputation. Time horizon and the Company’s ability to 
influence the outcome are also relevant.
The two views interact. A workforce or supply-chain issue can begin as a stakeholder impact and later affect 
quality, continuity and cash. An environmental investment can reduce operating cost and site risk while also 
lowering impact. A cyber or ethical failure can affect customers, employees, regulators and enterprise value at the 
same time.
Connect each matter to action
Management connection Required question Output
Strategy Which priority or Platform outcome 
can this matter change?Explicit strategic linkage
Risk and opportunity What can happen, how quickly and 
with what consequence?Scenario, appetite and response
Capital and operations Which decision, standard or 
investment changes the outcome?Owner, action and resource
Measurement Which leading and outcome 
evidence is reliable?Definition, target, boundary and 
control
Disclosure What do affected stakeholders need 
to understand?Balanced narrative and comparable 
indicators
This linkage prevents materiality from becoming an annual-report exercise. A matter is governed through the part 
of the organisation capable of changing it, with ESG and risk functions supporting consistency and the Board 
overseeing the most consequential trade-offs.
Refresh with the business
The Platform structure, Engineering Services Divestment Programme and expansion of physical capacity alter 
the context for several matters. Manufacturing may increase safety, environmental and supplier exposure. 
Productisation may increase IP , cybersecurity, reliability and lifecycle responsibilities. Portfolio change may increase 
employee, customer and governance sensitivity.
The final materiality view should therefore be validated against the Board-approved BRSR and refreshed when 
material transactions or operating changes occur. Stakeholders should be able to see not only which matters were 
selected, but why they matter now and how the Company intends to influence the outcome.

Governance and accountability
Responsible-business matters sit within the Company’s governance framework. The Chairman and 
Managing Director is the highest executive authority for these matters. Senior leadership, including 
the Managing Director and Chief Financial Officer, reviews ESG priorities, while the Board’s Risk 
Management Committee receives updates on ESG performance and developments. Enterprise 
functions set policies, standards and definitions; Platform and site teams apply them; and Board 
committees oversee performance in accordance with their mandates.
Financial controls, internal audit, the Code of Conduct, anti-corruption requirements and the vigil 
mechanism support accountability. AXISCADES uses the Business Responsibility and Sustainability 
Report (BRSR) to disclose policies, processes and performance under the nine principles of the 
National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct.The FY2026 Position
AXISCADES is connecting environmental, social and governance

delivery, customer trust, risk and long-term value.

SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY AND CSR
The Social Contract of 
AXISCADES 3.0: Empowering 
Communities Through 
Technology  
Our commitment to social responsibility is deeply integrated into our mission to deliver cutting-edge innovation and 
create value for all stakeholders. We recognise that our structural transition from a service provider to a high-fidelity 
technology and manufacturing platform carries a definitive social contract: to leverage our 15,000 man-years of 
expertise for the betterment of the communities in which we operate. 
Our approach is two-fold: ensuring the dignity and growth of our workforce - including those transitioning 
during our portfolio realignment - and driving impactful community interventions through our Corporate Social 
Responsibility (CSR) engine. Our CSR activities are overseen directly by the Board of Directors, ensuring that every 
rupee of expenditure is converted into measurable community progress.
Workforce Transformation: A People-Centric 
Migration
In Fiscal 2026, Management prioritised the “Power 930” 
roadmap’s most critical asset: our people. A significant milestone 
of the reporting period was the successful management of the 
Engineering Services Divestment Programme, which involved the 
planned transfer of approximately 2,200 employees to our strategic 
partner, Akkodis.
Dignified Transition:  The Group institutionalised a transparent 
framework for workforce management, ensuring that employees 
transferring with divested businesses did so with absolute clarity 
regarding their future roles and benefit structures.
A “Constructor” Skill Set:  For the core workforce remaining 
within our four growth platforms, the transition to a product-led 
mandate has been supported by intensive upskilling. This shift from 
man-hour intensive tasks to programme ownership and shop-floor 
discipline resulted in record operational productivity, with Revenue 
per Employee rising to `39.94 Lakh in FY2026. This successfully 
decoupled our growth potential from headcount expansion.

GOVERNANCE AND ETHICS
The Governance Foundation 
of AXISCADES 3.0
At AXISCADES, governance is viewed as the essential architecture that enables our structural transition from a service-led engineering 
house to a high-fidelity technology and manufacturing powerhouse. As we execute the “Power 930” roadmap, our governance framework 
ensures that every strategic move—from capital reallocation to the build-out of Atmanirbhar clusters is underpinned by transparency, 
accountability, and the highest standards of ethical conduct. We believe that robust governance is not merely a compliance requirement 
but a competitive advantage that builds long-term trust with our global Tier-1 OEMs, sovereign defence institutions, and shareholders.
Board Oversight and Strategic Stewards
The Board of Directors serves as the apex body for strategic supervision and risk oversight. In Fiscal 2026, 
the Board maintained a high state of alertness regarding the Group’s fundamental re-architecture. Central 
to this was the oversight of the Engineering Services Divestment Programme, a multi-year strategy to unlock 
“strategic fuel” for our product-led expansion.
The Board’s stewardship in FY2026 was characterised by:
• Disciplined Capital Allocation: Ensuring that the expected divestment proceeds are surgically directed 
toward high-margin growth engines: Aerospace, Defence, Electronics & AI (via XiDA Inc), and Space.
• Execution Monitoring:  Institutionalising the Strategy-to-Execution Scorecard to track high-fidelity 
evidence across programme delivery, capacity utilisation, and cash conversion.
• Structural Realignment:  Overseeing the consolidation of operations into four clear growth platforms to 
ensure specialized resource deployment and clearer performance accountability.
Commitment to Integrity and Ethical Conduct
Ethical behaviour is the cornerstone of the AXISCADES culture. The Group operates under a comprehensive 
Code of Conduct that applies to all Board members, senior management, and employees globally. This code 
is reinforced through regular induction and sensitization programs, ensuring that our 15,000 man-years of 
domain expertise are delivered with unwavering integrity.
• Anti-Corruption and Anti-Bribery: AXISCADES maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward any form of 
unethical business practice. Our robust framework prohibits the acceptance of personal payments or gifts 
that could impair objective judgment, ensuring that all business dealings are conducted at arm’s length.
• Whistle-blower Mechanism:  We have institutionalised a secure and transparent Vigil Mechanism. This 
platform empowers employees and stakeholders to report concerns regarding unethical behavior or 
policy violations directly to the Audit Committee, with absolute assurance of confidentiality and protection 
against retaliation.
• Human Rights:  In alignment with global standards, AXISCADES upholds universal human rights across 
its entire supply chain. Our employment practices are built on respect, fairness, and the prohibition of any 
form of forced or child labour.
Proactive Compliance and Regulatory Alertness
Management remains vigilant in maintaining the highest standards of corporate governance and regulatory 
compliance. During the reporting period, the Company proactively addressed administrative non-compliance 
relating to Board composition by remitting the requisite fines and taking immediate steps to evaluate suitable 
candidates to fill vacancies. The Board continues to emphasise diligent evaluations to ensure our leadership 
bench possesses the requisite multi-disciplinary expertise required for the Group’s manufacturing mandate.
Risk Management and Transparency
Governance at AXISCADES is deeply integrated with our Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) Framework. 
By identifying and tracking material issues—ranging from data privacy and cybersecurity to energy 
management—the Board ensures that sustainability and performance are balanced. This transparency is 
further evidenced by our commitment to providing a “published-to-comparable bridge” in future reporting, 
ensuring that stakeholders can clearly track the performance of continuing operations as our portfolio 
perimeter evolves.
Late event during the first quarter of FY2027: Following the formal conclusion of the Phase 2 divestment 
in June 2026, the Board has definitively formalised the Group’s structural transformation into a focused 
global platform. This transition is supported by a refreshed governance baseline, ensuring that our pure-
play manufacturing and technology operations are measured against the most stringent global standards of 
transparency and ethical excellence.

How the framework operates
1.Identify.  Business and functional teams identify strategic, 
financial, operational, regulatory, technology, people and 
external risks arising from existing activities and planned 
initiatives
2.Assess.  Risks are evaluated for likelihood, potential impact, 
velocity, interdependence and the strength of existing 
controls
3.Respond.  Owners define avoidance, reduction, transfer or 
acceptance measures, supported by clear timelines and 
accountability
4.Monitor.  Leading and lagging indicators are reviewed 
through business, programme, finance, quality and 
leadership forums
5.Report and escalate.  Material movements, control gaps 
and emerging risks are escalated to senior management and 
the Board or its committees, as appropriate
FY2026 risk context
FY2026 combined solid growth in the core domains with 
investment in manufacturing, testing, strategic systems and new 
operating platforms. The year also demonstrated the greater 
interdependence of procurement, production, inspection, customer 
acceptance, invoicing and collection in a manufacturing-linked 
model. This experience has reinforced the need for earlier visibility 
of constrained inputs, tighter programme-level planning and a more 
integrated order-to-cash rhythm.
Principal risks and management response
Principal risk Why it matters Management response
Portfolio 
transitionThe planned exit from legacy engineering-
services activities changes the Group’s 
operating perimeter, shared-service needs, 
workforce configuration and customer mix.Ring-fenced transition planning; coordination of corporate 
approvals and jurisdiction-specific requirements; governance for 
customer and employee continuity; knowledge-transfer protocols; 
strengthening of retained corporate and enabling functions; 
disciplined separation of systems, controls and accountabilities.
Programme 
execution 
and customer 
acceptanceComplex Aerospace and Defence 
programmes involve multiple milestones 
across design, sourcing, production, 
inspection, qualification and acceptance. 
Delays can shift revenue and cash across 
reporting periods.Programme-level ownership; integrated milestone planning; earlier 
alignment of inspection and acceptance windows; configuration 
control; cross-functional reviews covering delivery, invoicing and 
collection; escalation of exceptions against agreed thresholds.Financial and liquidity risk evidence
The transition towards manufacturing-linked delivery was reflected 
in the Company’s FY2026 cash profile. Working capital absorbed 
`156.84 crore during the year, debtor days increased from 107 
to 130, and net cash used in operating activities was `1.36 crore 
compared with `88.34 crore generated in the previous year. Net 
debt increased to `230.98 crore, while the current ratio moderated 
from 2.22 to 1.53.
These movements sharpen the operating priorities for the next 
phase: convert programmes into dispatch and acceptance, 
accelerate invoicing and collections, maintain appropriate buffers 
for critical inputs, and sequence capital expenditure against visible 
customer demand. The Company’s approach is to preserve 
strategic investment capacity while improving cash conversion and 
balance-sheet resilience.Risk culture and assurance
Effective risk management depends on 
behaviour as much as process. Leaders 
are expected to surface issues early, 
distinguish opportunity from committed 
revenue, challenge optimistic assumptions 
and maintain clear evidence for programme 
status. The control environment is 
supported by policies, delegation of 
authority, financial controls, quality systems, 
internal audit and independent statutory 
assurance.
The framework will continue to evolve 
with the Company’s operating perimeter. 
As AXISCADES becomes more focused, 
its risk management must become more 
granular at programme level and more 
connected across commercial, technical, 
operational and financial decisions.

RISK, OPPORTUNITY AND STRATEGY LINKAGE
Connecting strategic 
ambition with executionStructural opportunities within the chosen 
domains
Aerospace
Large global aircraft backlogs, supply-chain diversification 
and increasing demand for engineering-to-build participation 
create an opportunity for Indian suppliers with certified quality, 
cost competitiveness and programme credibility. AXISCADES 
is positioning for deeper participation in tooling, precision 
manufacturing, electrical systems, composites, supply-chain 
management and component MRO.
Defence
India’s focus on indigenous procurement and domestic capability 
creation supports long-duration opportunity in strategic electronics, 
missile and radar subsystems, land systems, test platforms and 
system integration. The Company’s opportunity is to move from 
design and subassembly positions towards repeat production and 
complete-system responsibility.
Electronics & AI
The convergence of semiconductors, embedded systems, 
thermal management, hardware realisation and AI infrastructure 
creates demand for partners that can connect design with 
testing and production. AXISCADES is building this as a scalable 
platform combining engineering depth, laboratories, electronics 
manufacturing and stronger international customer proximity.
Space
Commercialisation of the space economy and India’s expanding 
ecosystem create opportunity in satellite-bus manufacturing, 
payload and platform integration, space situational awareness 
and associated engineering. The Company is following a selective 
partnership-led approach, supported where appropriate by shared 
Aerospace and Defence capabilities.
Execution gates for opportunity capture
• Qualified demand:  a clearly defined customer need, 
commercial pathway and programme sponsor.
• Technical readiness:  validated design, certification route, bill 
of materials and manufacturing process.
• Capacity readiness:  appropriate facility, equipment, tooling, 
people and supplier ecosystem.
• Delivery readiness: integrated planning for procurement, 
production, inspection, acceptance and configuration control.
• Cash readiness: working-capital requirement, billing 
milestones, collection pathway and downside scenario.
• Governance readiness:  ownership, performance indicators, 
escalation thresholds and Board visibility where material.Indicators that matter
As the operating model evolves, 
management’s focus is moving from 
the size of the opportunity alone to the 
evidence of conversion. The most relevant 
indicators include the quality and maturity 
of the pipeline; programme conversion; 
on-time delivery and customer acceptance; 
capacity commissioning and utilisation; 
quality and safety performance; working-
capital intensity and cash conversion; 
and the readiness of critical talent and 
leadership roles.
Late event during the first quarter of 
FY2027
Following the reporting date, AXISCADES 
advanced the multi-stage divestment of 
its legacy Engineering Services business 
to Akkodis. The transaction formalised 
a sharper operating architecture around 
Aerospace Manufacturing, supply-chain 
management and MRO; Defence Solutions; 
the AI-centred Electronics & AI platform 
under XiDA Inc; and Space.
The transaction is strategically important 
because it can release capital and 
management capacity for the selected 
platforms. It also introduces transition 
requirements relating to employee 
movement, knowledge transfer, customer 
continuity, shared services, financial 
controls and the disciplined deployment of 
proceeds. Its multi-jurisdictional structure 
requires coordinated corporate approvals, 
consistent governance across subsidiaries, 
jurisdiction-specific compliance and 
transparent reporting through the residual 
ownership and transition period. These 
developments occurred after 31 March 
2026 and do not form part of the FY2026 
financial performance.AXISCADES views risk and opportunity as two sides of the same strategic choice. Structural demand in Aerospace, 
Defence, Electronics & AI and Space can support durable growth, but only where the Company can secure 
qualified programmes, commission the right capabilities, execute to exacting standards and convert delivery into 
cash. The strategy-to-risk linkage is therefore built around disciplined gates rather than unconstrained expansion.

BOARD OF DIRECTORS
Stewardship for a sharper 
enterprise
The Board provides strategic direction, 
governance oversight and independent 
challenge as AXISCADES reshapes its 
portfolio and builds a more focused 
technology and manufacturing platform. 
Its role is to ensure that the Company’s 
ambition is supported by sound capital 
allocation, transparent risk management, 
ethical conduct and clear accountability.
Governance philosophy
AXISCADES seeks to conduct business 
with integrity, fairness, transparency 
and respect for all stakeholders. The 
Board sets the tone for this culture and 
oversees the systems through which 
strategy, performance, risk, compliance 
and stakeholder interests are considered 
together. The governance framework is 
designed to support informed decisions, 
timely escalation and responsible long-term 
value creation
Compliance is the 
foundation. Good 
governance goes 
further: it shapes 
how decisions are 
made, how risks are 
managed and how 
stakeholder interests 
are balanced.Board oversight in FY2026
FY2026 required the Board to balance near-term performance 
with the design of a structurally different enterprise. The Board’s 
principal areas of attention included:
• Portfolio transformation:  reviewing the rationale, structure 
and execution pathway for the Engineering Services Divestment 
Programme.
• Capital allocation:  overseeing investment in facilities, 
manufacturing, testing, technology and strategic capabilities, 
with an emphasis on staged deployment and expected returns.
• Operational execution:  monitoring programme delivery, 
supply-chain constraints, customer acceptance, working capital 
and cash conversion.
• Strategic growth platforms:  guiding the consolidation  
of activities around Aerospace, Defence, Electronics & AI  
and Space.
• Risk and compliance:  reviewing material enterprise risks, 
internal controls, statutory obligations, ethical conduct and the 
effectiveness of remediation.
• People and leadership: considering organisational capability, 
succession, employee continuity and the skills required for a 
manufacturing- and systems-led operating model.
Governing strategic transformation
During this period, the Board’s role extended beyond conventional 
oversight. It acted as a strategic partner while retaining the 
independence and discipline required to test management 
proposals. Detailed deliberation on the long-term implications of 
portfolio choices, stakeholder impact, execution dependencies 
and downside scenarios helped balance strategic ambition with 
accountability and transparency.
The Engineering Services Divestment Programme is a complex 
restructuring spanning multiple subsidiaries, jurisdictions and 
legal frameworks across India, Europe and North America. 
Governance of the transaction requires the alignment of Board 
and, where applicable, shareholder approvals; securities-law 
obligations; entity-level actions; stakeholder communications; and 
consistent governance standards. The secretarial function works 
with management, finance, legal advisers, transaction teams and 
overseas subsidiaries to maintain this alignment without disrupting 
business continuity.Board capability and composition
The Board’s collective experience spans strategy, aerospace 
and defence, technology, manufacturing, finance, mergers and 
acquisitions, corporate law and governance. This blend is important 
in a year when the Company is simultaneously managing a 
strategic transaction, investing in new capacity and increasing its 
exposure to regulated, high-reliability domains.
Effective 23 August 2025, Dr. Sampath Ravinarayanan was 
appointed Managing Director, designated as Chairman, for a five-
year term. His sector experience and long-standing engagement 
with India’s aerospace and defence ecosystem provide continuity 
of strategic direction during the Company’s transformation.
Board effectiveness and information quality
As the Company evolves towards manufacturing, technology and 
AI-led platforms, governance capabilities must develop at the 
same pace. The secretarial function supports Board effectiveness 
by strengthening meeting processes, enabling discussion of 
technology governance and future capability requirements, and 
ensuring that directors receive timely, decision-useful information in 
a rapidly changing operating environment.
During the year, the Company addressed a period of administrative 
non-compliance relating to applicable Board-composition 
requirements, paid the levies prescribed by the stock exchanges 
and progressed the process of restoring the required composition. 
The matter reinforced the importance of succession planning, 
timely appointments and continued attention to the evolving 
governance obligations of a listed company.
The Board and its committees receive periodic information on 
financial performance, operations, material programmes, capital 
expenditure, risks, compliance, people and stakeholder matters. 
The quality of governance depends on complete and timely 
information, constructive challenge, clear minutes and follow-
through on agreed actions. These disciplines remain central to the 
Board’s effectiveness.
Subsidiary governance for a global Group
The Group’s expanding international footprint, new subsidiaries, 
manufacturing platforms and strategic partnerships require 
governance that is globally consistent and locally responsive. 
AXISCADES is working to maintain common standards of ethics, 
compliance, transparency and accountability across the Group, 
while recognising that each jurisdiction carries distinct legal, 
regulatory and reporting obligations.
This approach includes clearer entity-level accountability, alignment 
of subsidiary actions with Group strategy, appropriate reporting to 
the parent Board and coordination between local management, 
finance, legal and secretarial teams. Strong subsidiary governance 
is particularly important when programmes, intellectual property, 
employees and financial interests span more than one jurisdiction.Transparent and equitable 
shareholder communication
Regulatory compliance establishes 
the minimum standard for disclosure; 
shareholder confidence requires 
information that is also timely, accurate, 
consistent and meaningful. Stock-exchange 
filings, investor communications and the 
Annual Report are therefore treated as 
extensions of the governance framework. 
The objective is to explain the strategic 
rationale for material decisions, reduce 
information asymmetry and provide 
equitable access to information for all 
shareholders.
Strategic stewardship beyond 
the balance sheet
The Board’s stewardship extends to 
the capabilities that sustain long-term 
competitiveness: qualified people, 
customer trust, intellectual property, 
certified processes, supplier relationships, 
safety culture and institutional reputation. 
By overseeing these resources alongside 
financial capital, the Board supports a 
more complete view of value creation and 
resilience.
Looking ahead, the governance agenda will 
centre on Board effectiveness, strategic risk 
oversight, subsidiary and AI governance, 
succession planning, ESG integration and 
stakeholder engagement.

LEADERSHIP TEAM
Execution leadership  
across the chosen platforms
AXISCADES is led by a team with experience across strategy, finance, operations, Aerospace, Defence, Electronics 
& AI and international markets. The leadership mandate is to translate sharper strategic choices into programme 
conversion, qualified capacity, stronger cash generation and consistent stakeholder outcomes.
Leadership profilesA connected operating cadence
The leadership model is designed to combine platform 
accountability with strong functional coordination. Strategy, growth, 
operations, finance, supply chain, quality, people, technology and 
compliance must work from a shared view of programme status 
and risk. This is particularly important where the same decision 
affects delivery timing, capacity, working capital and  
customer confidence.
The executive agenda therefore centres on a small number of 
connected outcomes: convert qualified opportunities into orders; 
move orders through production and customer acceptance; 
commission capacity against demand; improve cash conversion; 
protect quality, safety and compliance; and build the leadership 
and specialist skills required for scale.
Capabilities strengthened during FY2026
The operating base broadened during the year. In Defence, the 
Company progressed new capabilities across strategic electronics, 
missile-related subsystems, land systems and mobile platforms, 
supported by a combination of owned capability and qualified 
partner ecosystems. In Electronics & AI, the Devanahalli facility 
added electronics assembly, acoustic testing and laboratory 
infrastructure. In Aerospace, capability development continued  
in tooling, electrical interconnection systems and initial 
manufacturing programmes.
The Company also began configuring a more unified customer 
relationship management environment during FY2026, including 
initial licences, system configuration and user training. This 
forms part of a wider objective to connect customer opportunity, 
programme delivery, procurement, invoicing and collection through 
stronger management information and clearer ownership.
Continuity through the portfolio transition
The divested and retained businesses have largely distinct 
customers and delivery structures, which reduces direct 
programme disruption. The transition nevertheless requires 
careful relocation of teams and reinforcement of retained functions 
across finance, human resources, talent acquisition, information 
technology and corporate operations. Leadership oversight is 
focused on preserving service continuity while ensuring that  
the retained organisation is appropriately resourced for its  
new perimeter.

Performance Review and  
Growth Strategy   
1. Economic Environment
1.1 Global Economy
The year closed with a global economy shaped by two opposing 
forces. One was a supply shock caused by the war in the Middle 
East while the other was a technology shock driven by artificial 
intelligence. Their effects were uneven. Economies inside the 
technology value chain outperformed; commodity importers 
outside it did not. For a company focused on defence, aerospace, 
space and deep-tech manufacturing, both forces run in the same 
commercial direction. Overall, global growth remained moderate 
through the reporting period, while geopolitical tension, supply-
chain fragility and accelerated investment in AI-related infrastructure 
shaped the outlook at the report date.
1.1.1 Growth, Inflation and Monetary Conditions
Global growth is projected at 3.0% in Calendar Year (CY) 2026 and 
3.4% in 2027, against a 3.5% average across 2024-25. Advanced 
economies expanded by 1.7% and emerging markets 3.8%. World 
trade volume growth slowed from 5.0% to 3.5% before recovering to 
4.3%. Tariffs and the re-routing of production chains accounted for 
most of that slowdown.
Inflation matters more for capital planning, and it has bottomed out. 
Global headline inflation is expected to rise from 4.1% in 2025 to 
4.7% in 2026, easing to 3.9% in 2027. Core inflation is expected to 
return to target only gradually: end-2027 in the United States and 
Japan, and 2028 in the euro area. Monetary conditions have turned 
less supportive. Expected policy rate paths have moved higher, in 
some cases flipping from cuts to hikes, and long-term sovereign 
yields have risen.

1.2 Indian Economy
India remained one of the faster-growing major economies during 
FY2026, supported by domestic demand, manufacturing and 
services.
1.2.1 FY2026 Context and Report-Date Outlook
Real GDP grew 7.7% in FY2026, supported by manufacturing, 
services, consumption and investment demand. The operating 
context was reinforced by elevated manufacturing capacity 
utilisation and continued investment in industrial capacity.
At the report date, the RBI projected real GDP growth of 6.6% and 
CPI inflation of 5.1% for FY2027, while maintaining the policy repo 
rate at 5.25% in June 2026. FY2027 projections remain subject to

For AXISCADES, the principal linkage is to capital expenditure,

qualification and execution.

1.2.2 Strategic Policy and Industrial Tailwinds
The fiscal stance remains expansionary in capital terms. Public 
capital expenditure rose from `11.2 lakh crore in BE (Budget 
Estimate) 2025-26 to `12.2 lakh crore in FY2026-27, while the fiscal 
deficit narrows to 4.3% of GDP and the debt-to-GDP ratio to 55.6%. 
Delivery of actual execution and disbursement of Public Capital 
Expenditure is running ahead of budget. Central government 
capital expenditure grew 18.8% year-on-year in April 2026, led 
by roads, railways, telecommunications and defence, and capital 
expenditure by large central public sector enterprises rose 63% 
year-on-year in the same month. Public capital expenditure and 
industrial policy continued to support manufacturing, infrastructure 
and strategic sectors. Budget measures aimed at strengthening 
electronics manufacturing, semiconductor capability, high-precision 
tooling, and critical components for aerospace and defence create 
a constructive medium-term backdrop.

design, test and manufacture high-precision components at scale.
Two measures bear directly on aerospace and defence 
manufacturing. Basic customs duty on components and parts for 
the manufacture of civilian, training and other aircraft is exempted. 
So is basic customs duty on raw materials imported for the 
manufacture of aircraft parts used in maintenance, repair and 
overhaul by units in the defence sector. On emerging technology, 
the Budget named the AI Mission, the National Quantum Mission, 
the Anusandhan National Research Fund and the Research, 
Development and Innovation Fund as the instruments through 
which new technologies are to be supported. 
1.2.3 Strategic Trade: Indo-US Engagement
India’s external position strengthened through a difficult year. Total 
exports reached USD 82 billion in May 2026, up 15.8% year-on-
year, with merchandise exports at a record USD 45.2 billion, up 
18.0%. Growth was broad-based. Engineering goods rose 24.5% 
and electronic goods 11.6%, and non-petroleum, non-gems-and-
jewellery shipments made up 75.8% of merchandise exports. 
India’s trade and investment position remained supportive, with 
engineering and electronics exports contributing to the broader 
manufacturing base.
India’s trade architecture is also being rebuilt in parallel, with new 
agreements, tariff developments and critical-mineral partnerships 
increasingly shaping the external environment for advanced 
manufacturing. The interim trade deal with the United States 
was announced in February 2026, while re-negotiations have 
continued since April, and although the US effective tariff rate 
has declined from around 14% earlier in the year to around 12%, 
policy uncertainty remains elevated following the temporary 10% 
surcharge on imports from India, introduced after a US Supreme 
Court ruling on tariffs imposed under international economic 
emergency powers and scheduled to expire in late July. Alongside 
this, India and the United States signed a bilateral Framework on 
Securing of Supply in the Mining and Processing of Critical Minerals 
and Rare Earths, while India and the United Kingdom launched a 
Critical Minerals Global Supply Chain Observatory, both of which 
support the National Critical Mineral Mission. The India-Oman 
CEPA entered into force on 1 June 2026 and the India-UK CETA on 
15 July 2026, reinforcing the broader shift towards more structured 
trade corridors, supply-chain resilience and improved access to 
strategic inputs. For companies operating in aerospace, defence, 
electronics and advanced engineering, these developments may 
influence market access, sourcing decisions, input availability and 
long-term supply-chain configuration.Capital flows reflected the same strategic recalibration. 
Gross foreign direct investment reached a historical 
peak of USD 94.5 billion in 2025-26, an increase of 
17.3%, while net FDI rose to USD 7.7 billion from USD 
1.0 billion, indicating continued long-term investor 
interest in India’s structural growth story. Foreign 
exchange reserves stood at USD 682.3 billion at end-
May 2026, equivalent to nearly eleven months of import 
cover, providing an important macroeconomic buffer at 
a time when portfolio flows remained more volatile, with 
net outflows of USD 13.7 billion between 1 April and 2 
June 2026.
This investment interest is also beginning to extend 
deeper into the aerospace value chain. Rolls-Royce is 
reported to be exploring an aero-engine maintenance, 
repair and overhaul facility in India and has also 
proposed an aero gas turbine complex to support 
indigenous engine development for future military 
aircraft programmes, underscoring the growing 
strategic relevance of India’s aerospace, defence and 
high-precision manufacturing ecosystem.

2. Industry Landscape, Outlook and Positioning
2.1 Aerospace, Manufacturing, SCM & MRO
2.1.1 Market Direction, Constraints and Relevance
Demand for air transport is expanding on every measure that 
matters to an aircraft manufacturer. Some 5.2 billion passengers 
are expected to fly in 2026, an increase of 4.4% on a 2025 that itself 
carried nearly five billion travellers across 38.7 million flights. Air 
cargo is forecast to reach 71.6 million tonnes, up 2.4%. Passenger 
traffic grew 5.7% in 2025 and load factors reached a record 
83.5%. Aircraft are flying fuller than at any point in the industry’s 
history, which is the clearest available signal that the existing fleet 
is being worked to its limit. Global air-transport demand and the 
commercial-aircraft backlog continue to support a long-duration 
production and aftermarket cycle. Passenger volumes are expected 
to rise, while the order backlog represents several years of current 
production capacity. Ageing fleets also support maintenance, repair 
and overhaul demand.

Ground infrastructure is already absorbing the strain. An average

India is gaining relevance as global aerospace original equipment 
manufacturers diversify engineering, manufacturing and sourcing.

base and a large domestic aviation market, creating opportunities 
in electrical systems, structures, precision components, supply-

During calendar 2025, global commercial aerospace revenue 
was projected to grow by around 12% year-on-year, supported by 
an estimated 25% increase in aircraft deliveries. North America 
was expected to expand by 17%, its strongest growth in over two 
decades, while Asia-Pacific and Europe were projected to grow 
by around 10% and 6%, respectively. Airbus targeted 820 aircraft 
deliveries for the year, while Boeing recorded its best first-half 
delivery performance since 2018. However, industry conversion 
continued to be constrained by certification timelines, specialised 
material availability, engine and component supply, skilled labour 
capacity and customer acceptance processes. For AXISCADES, 
this environment reinforces the opportunity to progress from 
engineering participation into qualified manufacturing, systems 
integration, supply-chain management and life support.

The geography of that spending is shifting. European growth 
continued at record levels, and the region now accounts for over 
21% of the global total, up from 17% in 2022. Russian expenditure 
moderated sharply, growing 3% in real terms in 2025 against 
56.9% in 2024, but still consumed over 7.3% of GDP . In the Middle 
East, regional spending has grown significantly since 2023. In 
Asia, concerns over China’s regional ambitions continue to drive 
modernisation, with China’s share of regional spending rising as its 
budget outpaces the wider region. At market exchange rates, the 
United States remains dominant at USD 921 billion. In purchasing-
power terms, both China and Russia are estimated to spend 
roughly double their headline figures. 
Europe has moved from spending to structure. The Readiness 
2030 plan proposes EUR 800 billion, of which member states may 
borrow up to EUR 650 billion nationally, with EUR 150 billion offered 
as loans for common procurement under the SAFE instrument. That instrument was oversubscribed by the states that 
took it up. Venture funding for European defence start-
ups has exceeded EUR 2.4 billion, the majority raised 
in 2025, and military space contracting is accelerating 
from a low base. 
India’s policy framework prioritises domestic design, 
development and manufacturing, supported by higher 
capital outlay, domestic-procurement preferences 
and an expanding private supplier ecosystem. These 
measures create multi-year opportunity, but approvals 
do not become executable revenue until procurement, 
contracting and qualification milestones are completed. 
For AXISCADES, the relevant opportunity spans

The global semiconductor industry is architected for a historic

Future of India’s Semiconductor IndustryBeneath the headline sits a structural divergence that matters more 
than the total. High-value AI chips now account for roughly half 
of industry revenue but represent less than 0.2% of unit volume. 
Around 1.05 trillion chips were sold in 2025 at an average selling 
price of USD 0.74, while generative AI accelerators number under 
20 million units. Chips for automotive, computers, smartphones and 
non-data-centre communications are growing considerably more 
slowly, and personal computing and smartphone sales are now 
expected to decline in 2026 as memory prices rise. 
India is building capability through semiconductor-design, 
packaging, electronics-manufacturing and incentive programmes. 
Its principal near-term advantage is a large design workforce; 
domestic fabrication remains an emerging capability, making 
integration, testing, embedded systems and advanced electronics 
the more immediate addressable areas.
The outlook for AXISCADES is sensitive to AI investment returns, 
memory prices, power availability, technology cycles and customer 
concentration. AXISCADES’ relevance lies in electronics design, 
assembly, testing, embedded computing and AI-enabled systems 
rather than in semiconductor fabrication itself.

PIB, June 20262.4 Space (Emerging Platform)
2.4.1 Market Direction, Constraints and Relevance
The global space economy continues to expand across satellite 
connectivity, launch services, navigation, Earth observation, 
ground systems and emerging in-orbit applications. The World 
Economic Forum and McKinsey estimated the space economy at 
USD 630 billion in 2023 and projected it to reach USD 1.8 trillion 
by 2035, covering both core “backbone” applications such as 
satellites, launchers and broadcast or GPS services, and wider 
“reach” applications where space technology enables revenues 
across other industries. More recent industry data from the Space 
Foundation estimated the global space economy at USD 613 billion 
in 2024, reflecting 7.8% year-on-year growth, with commercial 
activity accounting for the majority of the market. Growth is being 
supported by satellite broadband, positioning and navigation, Earth 
observation, AI-enabled analytics, sovereign space capability and 
expanding commercial launch activity. India is seeking a larger 
share of this opportunity through policy reform, private participation 
and investment in satellite, launch and ground-segment capability.
The structure of the sector favours specialists rather than only 
the largest players. Close to 80 space agencies now operate 
worldwide, including more than 70 national agencies and the space 
authorities of four US states, with over a quarter founded since 
2010. Only 16 have launch capability, and fewer still can recover 
payloads or support human spaceflight. While the three largest 
spenders command combined budgets estimated above USD 
50 billion annually, dozens of agencies operate between USD 1 
million and USD 1 billion and are looking for agile, cost-effective 
collaborators to close capability gaps. The ecosystem increasingly 
runs on public-private partnerships, collaborative research and 
flexible supply networks rather than on vertical integration. 
India’s space economy is currently valued at around USD 8 billion, 
about 2% of the global market. The Decadal Vision sets an ambition 
of USD 44.0 billion by 2033, roughly 8% of the global market, 
requiring a compound growth rate of 16%. Of that total, USD 33.0 
billion is expected from domestic demand growing at 14%, and 
USD 11.0 billion from exports growing at 38%. The segments move India’s space ecosystem is opening to private 
participation, but revenue conversion remains 
governed by authorisation, procurement 
cycles, programme maturity and capital 
discipline.at different speeds. Space-for-Earth, covering Earth observation, 
communication and navigation, rises from USD 7 billion to USD 
32.1 billion. Access-to-Space, covering satellite manufacturing, 
launch services and the ground segment, rises from USD 1.3 billion 
to USD 10.6 billion. Space-for-Space, covering space situational 
awareness and the in-orbit economy, rises from USD 0.1 billion to 
USD 1.3 billion.
Reform has been continuous rather than episodic. The Indian 
Space Policy 2023 was followed by an IN-SPACe seed fund 
scheme, liberalised foreign direct investment norms and formal 
authorisation procedures in 2024, a `1,000 crore venture capital 
fund and a `500 crore Technology Adoption Fund in 2025, and the 
transfer of Small Satellite Launch Vehicle technology to Hindustan 
Aeronautics Limited. The response is measurable. Space start-
ups have grown from one in 2014 to more than 400 as at February 
2026, attracting investment above USD 500 million, of which nearly 
USD 150 million came in 2025 alone. NewSpace India Limited 
revenues rose from `321.77 crore in FY2021-22 to `3,246.09 crore 
in FY2024-25. By 31 January 2026 IN-SPACe had facilitated 71 
technology transfers from ISRO to industry and start-ups, six non-
governmental entities had launched 18 satellites, and 25 payloads 
had flown or were scheduled on orbital experimental platforms.
Launch capacity is being built to match. India is self-reliant in space 
transportation to 10 tonnes in low Earth orbit and 4.2 tonnes to 
geosynchronous transfer orbit. A Next Generation Launch Vehicle 
has been approved with a 30-tonne capability to low Earth orbit 
and a partially reusable 14-tonne variant. A second spaceport is 
being developed at Kulasekarapattinam in Tamil Nadu; a dedicated 
Small Satellite Launch Vehicle complex is intended to support 20 
to 25 orbital launches annually, with the first launch targeted for 
FY2026-27; and a third launch pad at Sriharikota was approved 
in January 2025 at a cost of `3,984.86 crore. The stated strategic 
priority is for India to become a global hub for small satellites while 
achieving self-reliance in large satellites, with private manufacture of 
small launch vehicles and public-private partnership models for the 
larger ones.
For AXISCADES, the most relevant areas are selected space bus 
manufacturing, payload integrations, onboard computing, and 
space-situational-awareness applications. Space remains an 
emerging platform: procurement cycles are long, and investment 
remains dependent on partnerships and stage gates.
For a manufacturer with precision engineering, 
thermal and electronics capability, the 
addressable opportunity is in subsystems, 
ground infrastructure and satellite hardware 
rather than in launch vehicles.2.4.2 Outlook and Relevance to AXISCADES
India is seeking a larger share of this opportunity through 
policy reform, private participation and investment in 
satellite, launch and ground-segment capability. The 
Indian segment matching to Access-to-Space is forecast 
to compound at 20% to USD 10.6 billion by 2033. Space 
situational awareness grows faster still at 29%, though from 
a base of USD 0.1 billion. Both are infrastructure segments 
in which precision manufacturing, electronics and thermal 
capability, along with strategic partnerships with global 
space players with established space heritage are the 
qualifying credentials.
Three cautions apply. The absolute size remains small 
against the Company’s other platforms, so this is properly 
treated as an emerging position rather than a near-term 
revenue driver. Government demand dominates, and public 
procurement timelines are long. And the 16% compound 
rate assumes both that reform continues and that private 
capacity materialises to meet it, with the 38% export 
ambition the most demanding assumption in the plan.
2.5 Engineering R&D and Digital Engineering 
(Context)
India’s technology services sector generates around USD 
265 billion in annual revenue, close to 7% of GDP and 
roughly 20% of the USD 1.3 trillion global market. Growth 
has slowed to 4 to 5 per cent a year since the pandemic, 
with margins compressed by macroeconomic uncertainty, 
AI-led automation and intensifying competition. Measured 
against the 2035 aspiration of USD 750 billion to USD 850 
billion, current trajectories imply a shortfall of USD 250 
billion to USD 300 billion.
Engineering R&D is the faster-moving part of that picture. 
India’s ER&D exports stand at nearly USD 56 billion with 
the potential to reach USD 78 billion to USD 100 billion 
by FY2030. The addressable opportunity is a global R&D 
operations market of about USD 1.1 trillion, spanning 
automotive, medical technology, defence, semiconductors, 
industrials, energy and telecommunications. Positioning 
India as a hub for engineering R&D and innovation is 
assessed at USD 15 billion to USD 20 billion of potential by 
2035, with a further USD 10 billion to USD 15 billion from 
services built around frontier technologies including space 
and defence technology. MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION & ANALYSIS

Engineering Technologies Limited, is listed on the National Stock

31 March 2026, the Group comprised sixteen consolidated entities 
together with one associate, operating across India, the United 
States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Canada and China.
The Company’s history falls into three broad chapters. The 
founding era to 2015 built AXISCADES into an aerospace 
engineering services business, acquiring marquee original 
equipment manufacturer relationships and establishing a dedicated

period of consolidation, in which the founder stepped back from 
an executive role, an acquisition took the Company into defence

global aerospace. The foundation was preserved, but the growth

completed after 31 March 2026 are treated as post-year-end 
developments.
3.1.1 The Transition from Services to Products
The Group’s high-fidelity structural transition toward a product-led 
“Constructor” model is definitively recorded in the audited segment 
results for Fiscal 2026. Consolidated revenue from operations 
reached `1,158.95 crore, a performance underpinned by the rapid 
expansion of the mission-critical Defence Solutions platform. On 
the unaudited management domain view, Aerospace generated 
approximately `388 crore, Defence `378 crore and ESAI `136 crore 
in FY2026. 
The divergent trajectories between our four growth platforms and 
legacy services are evidenced by the following granular data points
• Defence Solutions Outperformance:  Revenue for the 
Defence segment grew by 24.7% to `377.70 crore (up from 
`302.90 crore in FY2025). More significantly, the segment 
result surged 90.9% to reach `82.86 crore, reflecting a 
dominant 21.9% segment margin.
• Technology Services and Solutions (TSS) Re-architecture: 
The TSS segment, which currently houses the legacy services 
being divested, recorded revenue growth of 7.3% to `781.30 
crore, but saw its segment result contract by 8.0% to `66.36 
crore, yielding a lower margin of 8.5%.
• Capital Reallocation and Asset Intensity:  In alignment with 
the “Power 930” roadmap, segment assets for Defence rose 
51% over the year to reach `577.12 crore, while TSS assets 
grew by a more moderate 19% to `615.63 crore. This shift 
is further mirrored in the liabilities, where Defence-related 
obligations rose by approximately 62% to `343.48 crore to 
support high-intensity delivery cycles for 21 active design 
wins.
• Contribution Mix:  Consequently, while Defence accounted for 
approximately 32.6% of consolidated revenue, it delivered over 
55% of the total segment result, confirming its status as the 
Group’s primary engine for value creation.Key commercial highlights for FY2026 include ~21 
active defence design and programme positions 
across airborne mission electronics; radar, air-defence 
and counter-UAS systems; maritime and electronic-
warfare systems; and integrated ground and test 
platforms. These positions span design, qualification, 
L1, production and formal-order stages and are 
presented separately from firm executable orders. The 
Company also secured its first integrated design-and-
manufacturing aerospace engagement.
The strategic objective for the Company is to increase 
its participation across the customer product lifecycle, 
from engineering and qualification to manufacturing, 
integration, testing and lifecycle support. The transition 
is expected to require greater working capital, 
qualification discipline and fixed-capital intensity before 
scale benefits emerge.
3.1.2 “Power 930” Vision
Power 930 is AXISCADES’ FY2030 ambition to build 
a `9,000 crore revenue enterprise with profit after tax 
of `960 crore. The vision is anchored in a deliberate 
shift from headcount-linked engineering services 
towards a higher-value portfolio of products, integrated 
solutions, manufacturing and IP-led offerings across 
Aerospace, Defence, ESAI and Space. The roadmap 
combines organic growth through programme 
conversion and capacity expansion with selective 
acquisitions, strategic partnerships and disciplined 
investment in manufacturing, integration, testing and 
MRO infrastructure. FY2026 represented an important 
foundation year, during which the Company sharpened 
its portfolio, expanded critical capabilities, strengthened 
its opportunity pipeline and began building the 
operating base required to progress from design 
engagements to qualified production and complete-
system responsibility. Delivery of the vision will depend 
on customer qualification, order conversion, timely 
capacity ramp-up, supply-chain resilience, acquisition 
integration, working-capital discipline and cash 
conversion. “Power 930” is a long-term management 
ambition, with progress assessed through measurable 
operating and financial milestones, rather than as a 
guarantee of future performance.

3.3 Leadership and Organisational Transformation
Dr. Sampath Ravinarayanan was re-designated Founder, Chairman 
and Managing Director, returning to executive leadership of the 
Company. Mr. Alfonso Martinez ceased to hold the position of  
Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director and was appointed

Managing Director of add solutions GmbH. Shashidhar S.K. 
continues as Group Chief Financial Officer.
Mr. Mukund Santhanam was appointed as the Chief Strategy and 
Growth Officer and designated as Senior Management Personnel 
(SMP) of the Company with effect from February 9, 2026. bringing 
three decades of experience in financial markets including a decade 
in the aviation sector. His remit spans organic and inorganic growth 
opportunities, and engagement with the investor community.
On 26 March 2026, the Board appointed Mr. Giridhar Aramane 
as Non-Executive Independent Director. An Indian Administrative 
Service officer of the 1988 batch, he served as Defence Secretary 
to the Government of India between 2022 and 2024, and previously 
as Secretary in the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and 
as Additional Secretary in the Cabinet Secretariat.
The total headcount remained structurally stable, rising from 
2,891 at the close of FY2025 to 2,902 on 31 March 2026. Within the FY2026 total core employees increased from 
1,637 to 1,792 and support staff from 246 to 288, 
while industrial employees reduced from 913 to 822, 
reflecting the operating model run with customers and 
the ramp-down of specific programmes. Attrition was 
~19% for the year. On completion of the restructuring, 
approximately 2,200 employees will transfer with the 
divested businesses.
3.4 Strategic Manufacturing & Integration 
Infrastructure: 
Scaling to Tier-1 System Responsibility
The Company is undergoing a fundamental structural 
transition, evolving from subsystem engineering 
towards full-scale manufacturing and system-
level responsibility. This evolution is anchored by 
a significant capital commitment into specialized, 
high-security infrastructure designed to meet the non-
discretionary requirements of global aerospace and 
defence mandates.
3.4.1 Devanahalli Atmanirbhar Complex (DAC): India’s 
Premier Private Defense Campus
The Devanahalli Atmanirbhar Complex represents a 
definitive scale advantage for the platform. Spanning 
a twenty-acre campus with approximately 3.12 million 
square feet of built-up area, this facility stands as one of 
the largest private-sector defence hubs in the nation.
The initial operational phase provides a comprehensive 
suite of common mission-critical facilities, including 
specialized hangars, electronics manufacturing lines, 
and advanced testing infrastructure. To support the 
high-fidelity requirements of modern warfare, the 
campus integrates dedicated anechoic chambers, 
high-velocity “speed shops,” and integrated offset 
management functions. Looking ahead, the complex 
is engineered to act as a global “Plug-and-Play” hub 
for Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs); the 
subsequent phase envisages four secure, build-to-
suit quarters dedicated to major international defence 
corridors, offering 2.4 million square feet of dedicated 
capacity for global partnership integration.
3.4.2 Missile Atmanirbhar Complex (MAC), 
Hyderabad: Transitioning to Strategic System 
Integration
In Hyderabad’s Aerospace Park, the Company 
is establishing a frontier facility focused on the 
manufacturing and integration of strategic missile 
components. Occupying eight acres, this complex 
is being developed in collaboration with a global 
technology leader to create one of India’s most 
advanced missile-system integration hubs.
With an indicative investment framework of `600 crore, 
this facility substantiates the Company’s migration 
toward high-value system-level responsibility. During MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION & ANALYSIS

Manufacture

margin profile of the retained aerospace business.
During FY2026, the Aerospace domain operated as an integrated 
platform comprising established engineering services and 
emerging capabilities in aerospace tooling, electrical systems, 
precision manufacturing and product realisation. Engineering teams 
continued to support global aerospace OEMs across design, 
analysis, modification, certification and lifecycle-engineering 
requirements. In parallel, the Company began establishing the

programme progression, production volumes, customer schedules, 
contractual milestones and acceptance requirements.

knowledge with tooling, manufacturing, supply-chain orchestration 
and lifecycle support. Its progression will depend on customer 
qualification, certification, initial ramp-up costs, capacity utilisation 
and the disciplined execution and integration of any inorganic 
capability additions.

4.2. Defence: Scaling Electronics, Systems and Platform 
Responsibility
Defence recorded the strongest FY2026 growth among the Group’s 
audited reportable segments. Segment revenue increased by 
24.7% to `377.70 crore, while segment result increased by 90.9% to 
`82.86 crore. Segment assets increased to `577.12 crore, reflecting 
the larger operating and working-capital base required to support 
manufacturing-led programme execution.
During the year, AXISCADES expanded its participation across 
airborne mission electronics, radar and air-defence systems, 
electronic warfare, maritime electronics, missile-related capabilities, 
land systems and integrated test platforms. The portfolio included 
21 active design and programme positions at different stages of 
development, qualification and production.
In airborne systems, the Company progressed control electronics, 
radar front-end and beam-control units, together with rugged 
radio-frequency and embedded-computing modules. In radar and 
air defence, it advanced digital beamforming, transmit-receive, 
signal-processing and counter-UAS architectures. Maritime and 
electronic-warfare activities included sonar processing, software-
defined electronic-intelligence receivers, antenna systems and 
specialised control electronics.
The strategic progression is from discrete design and subsystem 
engagements towards repeat production, greater integration 
responsibility and complete-system delivery. Revenue conversion 
will depend on qualification, production authorisation, critical-
component availability, delivery, inspection, customer acceptance 
and the applicable revenue-recognition criteria. Certain fourth-
quarter deliverables moved into FY2027 following supply-chain and 
programme-timing constraints.
Late event during the first quarter of FY2027. On 27 May 2026, 
AXISCADES secured an order from a national defence research 
organisation for the manufacture and supply of a deployable 
mission-mast system. The engagement represents an important 
progression from subsystem delivery towards complete-platform 
design, integration, qualification and manufacturing responsibility.
4.3. XiDA - ESAI: Extending from Engineering into Product 
Realisation
ESAI generated approximately `136 crore of revenue and `36 
crore of EBITDA in FY2026, representing a management-reported 
EBITDA margin of 26.1%.
During FY2026, AXISCADES expanded its electronics assembly, 
testing and acoustic-laboratory capabilities at Devanahalli Aero 
Land. Dedicated infrastructure supported deeper engagements 
across semiconductors, automotive electronics, consumer 
technology, embedded systems and artificial intelligence. These 
investments strengthened the Company’s ability to move beyond 
design services into prototyping, testing, hardware realisation and 
recurring production.
The strategic objective is to organise ESAI’s electronics, post-silicon 
engineering, embedded systems and AI capabilities into a more 
scalable, IP-led global platform. Near-term progress will depend on customer programme conversion, utilisation of the 
new infrastructure, repeat production volumes and 
disciplined integration of any acquired capabilities.
Late event during the first quarter of FY2027.  The 
Company announced the development of XiDA Inc 
as its US-headquartered platform for ESAI and AI. 
The initiative brings together the existing India and 
US operations and the Group’s AI capabilities. Any 
acquisition-related revenue, earnings or capability 
contribution will be recognised only after definitive 
agreements are executed, control is established and 
the relevant transaction closes.
4.4. Portfolio Engineering Services: FY2026 
Contribution before Divestment
The Automotive, Energy and Heavy Engineering 
businesses generated approximately `239 crore of 
revenue during FY2026. These operations remained 
active throughout the reporting period and formed 
part of the Group’s FY2026 Technology Services and 
Solutions segment.
The businesses continued to provide engineering 
and technology support to global customers across 
product development, industrial systems and lifecycle 
requirements. During the year, management also 
progressed a broader portfolio review intended to 
concentrate capital and leadership attention on 
Aerospace, Defence, ESAI and other manufacturing- 
and IP-led opportunities.
Late event during the first quarter of FY2027.  On 26 
May 2026, AXISCADES entered into agreements for 
the proposed transfer of these businesses to Akkodis. 
The disclosed transaction value was approximately 
US$30.63 million, comprising fixed consideration of 
US$23.23 million and an additional contingent earn-out. 
Completion remains subject to conditions precedent, 
regulatory approvals and customary adjustments.
This transaction represented the first phase of the 
Engineering Services Divestment Programme. It will 
alter the Group’s FY2027 operating and reporting 
perimeter but does not change the inclusion of these 
businesses within FY2026 performance.
4.5. Space: Establishing a Long-Term Strategic 
Platform
During FY2026, AXISCADES undertook preparatory 
work in selected space-related opportunities. Space 
did not have separately disclosed revenue during the 
year and remained at an early stage of commercial 
development.
The year’s activities included discussions with 
international partners regarding satellite-bus 
manufacturing and systems integration, together 
with progress on a space-situational-awareness collaboration. These opportunities draw upon capabilities 
already present within Aerospace, Defence and ESAI, including 
precision engineering, electronics, antennas, embedded systems, 
manufacturing and complex systems integration.
Late event during the first quarter of FY2027.  After the reporting 
date, AXISCADES formally positioned Space as a distinct 
strategic growth platform. Its proposed scope includes satellite-
bus manufacturing, integration, payload-related capabilities and 
space situational awareness. Commercial progress will depend on 
definitive partner agreements, customer programmes, regulatory 
requirements, investment gates and Board approval.
Reading FY2026 against the Future Portfolio
FY2026 reflects AXISCADES’ performance across its complete 
historical operating perimeter. The transactions announced during 
the first quarter of FY2027 establish a materially different future 
perimeter centred on Aerospace Manufacturing, Defence Solutions, 
XiDA / ESAI and Space.
As the relevant transactions progress and their accounting 
treatment is finalised, the Company will provide retained-perimeter 
and like-for-like disclosures to help investors assess the scale, 
margin profile, capital intensity and cash-generation characteristics 
of the transformed business.

demonstrating improved business mix and operating leverage.
Consolidated EBITDA increased by 24.6% to `177.51 crore from 
`142.44 crore. EBITDA margin expanded by 150 basis points to 
15.32%, compared with 13.82% in FY2025.
Profit before exceptional items and tax increased by 36.5% 
to `124.76 crore. After net exceptional items, profit before tax 
increased by 29.8% to `113.59 crore from `87.52 crore.
Defence made an institutional contribution to this performance, 
with segment revenue growing 24.7% to `377.70 crore. More 
significantly, its audited segment result increased by 90.9% to 
`82.86 crore, reflecting a dominant segment margin of 21.9%.
5.3. Understanding the PAT Outcome
Despite the strong growth in pre-exceptional earnings, consolidated 
profit after tax declined by 4.3% to `72.07 crore. The movement 
from pre-exceptional earnings to reported PAT is explained 
principally by exceptional items and the higher tax charge.
Net exceptional charge
FY2026 included net exceptional charges of `11.17 crore, compared 
with `3.86 crore in FY2025. The FY2026 amount comprised:
• `7.82 crore of past-service cost relating to gratuity and leave 
encashment following the notification of the new Central 
Labour Codes;• `7.98 crore of goodwill impairment; and
• a partly offsetting gain of `4.63 crore from 
the remeasurement of contingent purchase 
consideration.
Higher tax charge
The income-tax charge increased to `41.52 crore from 
`12.23 crore in FY2025. Consequently, the effective tax 
rate increased to approximately 36.6%, compared with 
approximately 14.0% in the previous year.
The FY2025 comparison base benefited from a 
current-tax reversal and deferred-tax credits following 
the completion of an income-tax assessment and the 
recognition of deferred tax assets. The higher FY2026 
effective tax rate is attributed to the jurisdictional mix of 
profits and the non-recognition of a deferred tax asset 
in a loss-making overseas entity.
The combination of the higher tax charge and net 
exceptional items more than offset the improvement 
in pre-exceptional earnings, resulting in the modest 
decline in reported PAT. Basic earnings per share 
consequently declined by 4.7% to `16.92.
Fourth-quarter programme timing
While Fiscal 2026 was marked by robust top-line 
performance and structural scaling, consolidated 
outcomes were affected by the timing of certain 
programme-linked milestones in the final quarter. 
Approximately `142 crore of programme-linked revenue, 
initially anticipated for recognition by 31 March 2026, 
was carried forward into the succeeding fiscal period, 
primarily due to supply-chain constraints, production 
timing, inspection schedules, customer-acceptance 
processes and transaction-related transition factors.
As AXISCADES progresses from engineering 
services towards qualified manufacturing, integration 
and lifecycle participation, revenue recognition is 
increasingly linked to physical delivery, qualification 
timelines, OEM-level inspection gates and customer 
acceptance, rather than only to engineering effort or 
man-hour deployment. During the fourth quarter, while 
throughput across key operating clusters remained 
strong, the timing of customer-acceptance schedules 
for certain advanced subsystems moved beyond the 
reporting date.
The related revenue and associated margins were 
therefore not recognised in the FY2026 audited 
results, with the estimated EBITDA impact relative 
to internal expectations exceeding `40 crore. This 
timing movement should be viewed as an operational 
carry-forward within the contract lifecycle, rather than 
as a statutory adjustment to reported Profit After 
Tax. The carry-forward forms part of the year-end 
executable order book and remains subject to delivery, MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION & ANALYSIS

Total equity increased by 12.0% to `734.44 crore at 31 March 2026, 
compared with `655.79 crore at the previous year-end. Total assets 
increased to `1,466.21 crore, reflecting investment in operating 
capacity and a larger working-capital base.
The year-end position was as follows:
• Gross borrowings, excluding lease liabilities, increased to 
`276.44 crore from `189.48 crore.
• Trade receivables increased to `411.34 crore from `301.80

5.5 Return on Net Worth
Return on net worth was 9.88% against 11.55%, computed as profit 
attributable to owners of the Company divided by closing equity 
attributable to owners. On average equity, the figure is 10.45%.
The decline of 167 basis points is arithmetic rather than operational. 
Profit attributable to owners fell 4.0% to `71.92 crore while equity 
attributable to owners grew 12.1% to `727.54 crore, the latter driven 
by retained earnings, the share-based payment charge and gains 
on translation of foreign operations. Normalised for exceptional 
items, return on net worth would be approximately 11.4%, broadly 
level with the prior year.
The measure will be materially affected in FY2027 by the 
extraordinary gain expected on completion of the divestment 
programme.6. Strategic Opportunities and 
Operational Challenges
The Company is currently executing a fundamental 
pivot under the AXISCADES 3.0 framework, 
transitioning from a manpower-intensive services 
model to a product-led manufacturing platform. This 
transformation is supported by significant sector 
tailwinds but requires disciplined management of near-

6.1 Strategic Opportunities
AXISCADES is positioned at the intersection of global 
aerospace scarcity and India’s indigenous defence 
surge. Conversion of these opportunities is being 
sequenced through disciplined capital deployment, 
phased capacity creation and rigorous customer-
qualification milestones across the Company’s new 
manufacturing clusters.
Strategic Opportunities: Re-Architecting for Non-
Linear Growth
The Company is currently executing a fundamental 
pivot under the AXISCADES 3.0 framework, 
transitioning from a manpower-intensive services 
model to a product-led manufacturing platform. This 
transformation is supported by significant sector 
tailwinds and structural shifts in global and domestic 
procurement.
• The Global Aerospace Super-Cycle: The global 
aircraft industry is entering an unprecedented 
super-cycle, evidenced by a combined order 
backlog exceeding 17,000 units, representing 
nearly twelve years of current production capacity. 
With industry normalisation not anticipated before 
2031, major global airframers have designated 
India as a primary destination for diversified Tier-1 
sourcing and manufacturing. AXISCADES is 
strategically positioned to capture this demand by 
pivoting from a service-led “architect” of designs 
to a product-led “constructor” of mission-critical 
assemblies. This structural shift allows the Group 
to leverage its 16-year pedigree of executive-level 
OEM trust to secure long-term, non-linear growth 
within the global aviation supply chain.
• India’s Formative Space Economy: India’s 
domestic space market is projected to expand 
significantly, reaching an estimated US$ 44 billion 
by 2033, with the high-value “Access-to-Space” 
segment compounding at a 20% CAGR. Our 
newly established Space Division is engineered to 
capture early-stage value by focusing on satellite 
bus structural manufacturing and integrated 
payload systems. By bypassing early-stage 
organic development through strategic JVs and 
partnerships, we are accelerating our entry into 
the commercial satellite integration market. This platform leverages our high-reliability aerospace foundation 
to provide a future-ready manufacturing engine for the 
burgeoning private space economy.
• Shared Manufacturing Architecture:  A cornerstone of the 
AXISCADES 3.0 transformation is our shared manufacturing 
architecture, anchored by the Devanahalli (DAC) and Missile 
(MAC) Atmanirbhar clusters. This unique framework utilises a 
common technology foundation—encompassing advanced 
composites, precision machining, and strategic electronics—
to serve three distinct demand streams: Aerospace, Defence, 
and Space. By consolidating manufacturing requirements into 
a single tri-use factory base, we create significant operating 
leverage and build a defensible technical moat. This structural 
efficiency ensures that capital deployment is maximised 
across multiple high-growth industries while accelerating our 
journey toward becoming a Tier-1 manufacturing partner.
• High-Velocity Defence Pipeline: Our Defence vertical is 
powered by a high-velocity portfolio that currently includes 
21 active design wins and strategic programme positions 
across air defence, electronic warfare, and surveillance. By 
aggressively migrating toward mission-ready “Systems & 
Solutions” (Stage 5), we are moving up the value chain to 
take full-cycle responsibility for integrated national defence 
platforms. This strategy is exemplified by our various 
prestigious wins, which reinforces our credentials as an 
indigenous precision manufacturing partner. This robust order 
pipeline provides clear revenue visibility and ensures that 
our Defence engine remains a primary driver of high-margin 
growth.
• ESAI Focus:  XiDA Inc. is AXISCADES’ US-led platform, 
established to support the Group’s expansion into Electronics, 
Semiconductors and Artificial Intelligence. The platform is 
intended to strengthen access to advanced engineering 
capabilities, deepen participation in the US technology 
ecosystem, and create opportunities across AI infrastructure, 
compute, memory and physical AI applications. By combining 
international technology capabilities with AXISCADES’ India-
based engineering and manufacturing ecosystem, XiDA is 
expected to support the development of repeatable, higher-
value solutions in fast-growing ESAI domains.
6.3.2 Operational Challenges and Risk Mitigation
The Group’s rapid scale-up and structural realignment present 
specific operational pressures that are being proactively addressed 
through the Power 930  capital-allocation framework.
• Working Capital and Liquidity Management: During 
Fiscal 2026, the Group’s strategic pivot toward high-value 
manufacturing clusters and long-cycle defence programs led 
to a significant `156.84 crore absorption of working capital, 
resulting in a temporary rise in net debt to `230.98 crore 
and an extension of debtor days to 130. While this deliberate 
deployment into long-cycle assets moderated our current 
ratio from 2.22 to 1.53, it represents an essential investment 
in the infrastructure required to anchor the AXISCADES 3.0 transformation. To mitigate these liquidity 
pressures and restore balance sheet efficiency, 
the Group has successfully concluded a 
two-phase Engineering Services Divestment 
Programme to the Akkodis Group, valued at 
approximately `2,256 crore. These proceeds, 
scheduled to flow in tranches beginning in the 
third quarter of FY2027, provide the necessary 
“dry powder” to fully fund our Power 930 growth 
roadmap while significantly reducing high-cost 
borrowings. This disciplined capital reallocation 
transforms our liquidity profile, ensuring that our 
journey toward a `9,000 crore revenue target is 
supported by a robust and fully funded financial 
foundation.
• Supply Chain Resilience:  Throughout Fiscal 
2026, AXISCADES successfully navigated global 
logistics disruptions and a nearly 90% surge in 
titanium prices across its integrated aerospace 
operations by pivoting toward a structural, IP-led 
supply chain strategy designed to insulate the 
“Power 930” growth roadmap. By leveraging 16 
years of executive-level OEM trust, the Group is 
qualifying for “Buy-Back” and “Flow-Through” 
procurement frameworks that grant access to raw 
materials at locked-in pricing, effectively shielding 
operating margins from extreme spot-market 
volatility. Furthermore, the Company’s “Mirroring 
Architecture” facilitates the direct transfer of 
sophisticated procurement and manufacturing 
IP from international acquisition targets into 
the newly established Devanahalli Atmanirbhar 
Cluster (DAC). This strategic embedding of 
advanced international techniques reduces raw 
material consumption per component, mitigating 
the financial impact of material inflation while 
strengthening domestic self-reliance under the 
Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative.
• Talent Transition and Attrition:  AXISCADES 
concluded Fiscal 2026 with an attrition rate 
of 19% while successfully navigating a large-
scale organizational recalibration driven by our 
strategic pivot toward high-value manufacturing. 
As part of the Engineering Services Divestment 
Programme, approximately 2,200 employees are 
scheduled to transition to the Akkodis Group, 
a move that definitively sharpens our internal 
focus on pure-play technology and production 
platforms. Management is maintaining an 
uncompromising focus on retaining “core” high-
potential talent, ensuring that our established 
engineering pedigree is concentrated within our 
hardware-driven AI and space manufacturing 
divisions. This disciplined approach to human 
capital ensures that our technical moats remain 
robust as we transition from a services firm into MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION & ANALYSIS
